text: The smoke test in Lesson 12 confirmed the environment you built actually works. That feels like the finish line, but a newly deployed environment with no monitoring configured is flying blind. Monitoring isn't a feature you bolt on once something breaks — it's part of the deployment itself, which is why this chapter starts right here.

Here's the difference that matters. A disk fills up slowly over a few days of log growth. With monitoring in place, an alert fires at 85% full, and someone frees space before anything breaks. Without monitoring, nobody knows until the disk hits 100%, the app crashes, and the first anyone hears about it is a user reporting the site is down. Same root cause, two completely different outcomes — one found from an alert, in advance, the other from a complaint, after the damage.

The VNets or VPCs, VMs or EC2 instances, and storage from Chapters 1 through 3 already started reporting platform metrics automatically the moment they existed, exactly as covered earlier in this program. That part needs no extra work. What doesn't happen automatically: nothing is watching those metrics, nothing notifies anyone when a threshold is crossed, and logs aren't flowing anywhere centralized yet.

The first concrete step, right after the smoke test, is creating the destination everything else in this chapter will attach to — a Log Analytics workspace in Azure, or a CloudWatch Log group in AWS. Every diagnostic extension, every agent, and every alert configured later points at one of these. Creating it now turns data the platform happens to be collecting into data someone can actually see.

Platform metrics being collected is not the same thing as monitoring being stood up — that's the gap this chapter closes before this environment takes on real traffic. Next up: configuring the handful of alerts that actually matter for a deployment like this one, instead of trying to alert on everything at once.
